They compare this with Homer's ancient hero Odysseus, seeing how one theme, coming home, appears in a myth and in a modern novel.","enduringUnderstanding":"Stories from different times and cultures explore shared ideas, such as home, but portray them differently because of characters' families, situations and values.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 35's Academic Discussion, students will use today's comparison and their annotations from the myths and The Lightning Thief to discuss how retellings change across cultures and generations.","performanceTask":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students compare two narratives to explain different views of a theme. Today they practice comparing two homecoming narratives with text evidence, transitions and a formal style."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"variation","definition":"a difference from the usual or standard form; in language, wording that is not standard English","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"conventional","definition":"following the accepted rules or the usual way of doing something, such as standard English grammar","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"contrast","definition":"to show how two things are different","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"depict","definition":"to show or describe something in a story, picture or other work","tier":"support"},{"word":"rejoice","definition":"to feel and show great happiness","tier":"support"},{"word":"nymph","definition":"in Greek myth, a female nature spirit who lives in a place such as a river, tree or cave","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"pp. 370-375"},{"title":"The Odyssey, Book 13 (excerpt)","author":"Homer","pages":"Odysseus recognizes Ithaca"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Spark thinking about what home means and connect it to the heroes' returns students will compare today.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"What Does Home Mean?","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Think about a time you came home after being away. Turn to a partner and describe how you felt and what made that place feel like home."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What makes a place feel like home: the place itself, the people in it, or something else?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I think it's the people. When I got back from my grandma's, I was happiest to see my little brother and my mom, not just my room."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Heroes in stories come home too. Today we compare two of them: Percy at the end of Chapter 22 and Odysseus in an ancient Greek poem. You will write about what home means to each."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep talk to about three minutes. Take one or two shares and move on; the heavy lifting comes later."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Teach students to recognize variations from standard English and use strategies to make their expression formal and conventional before they write about the texts.","activities":[{"id":"lab-standard-english","title":"Recognizing Variations from Standard English","minutes":10,"standards":["L.6.1","L.6.1.e"],"routine":"Language Study","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Writers use different language in different settings. Texting a friend, we might write 'Percy was like, so done with school.' In an explanatory paragraph, we use formal, standard English. A *variation* is wording that differs from the standard. Our strategy has three steps: spot it, reread it aloud, then revise it to *conventional* language. Look for slang, a shift in verb tense, a missing apostrophe or a vague word like 'stuff.'"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read each sentence about Chapter 22. With a partner, find the variation and rewrite the sentence in formal, standard English. Sentence 1: Percy was like totally unsure about going back to camp. Sentence 2: His mom picked a school that is good for him, so Percy decides to stay home. Sentence 3: Percy dont know if home is a place or his mom."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"I will model the first one. 'Like totally' is slang. I replace it with a precise word: 'Percy was uncertain about returning to camp.' I reread it aloud and it sounds formal and clear."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What variation did you find in Sentence 2, and how did you fix it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The verbs switch tense. 'Picked' is past and 'decides' is present. I changed it to 'picks' so it says, 'His mom picks a school that is good for him, so Percy decides to stay home.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What about Sentence 3?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"'Dont' is missing an apostrophe, and with 'Percy' it should be 'doesn't.' I also changed 'mom' to 'mother' to sound more formal. 'Percy doesn't know if home is a place or his mother.'"},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Focus on strategies, not on correcting students' home language. Present formal English as the right choice for this task and audience, not as better than other ways of speaking."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"As you write today, use this check: read your sentence aloud, listen for slang or a tense shift, and revise it to be formal and conventional."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students notice differences between informal and formal English and add detail to sentences with adverbials.","sayAsk":"Say: Informal is how we talk with friends. Formal is how we write for school. Ask: Which word sounds informal? What is a more formal word? Frames: The word ___ is informal. A more formal way to say it is ___. Expand a sentence with where, when or why: Percy thinks about home ___ (in the final chapter / with his mother / because he misses her).","watchFor":"If students only copy the corrected sentence, then ask them to say why the first version did not fit formal writing. If students add details unrelated to the text, then point back to Chapter 22 and ask where, when or why for Percy. Success: students identify a variation and revise it orally or in writing."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: spotting variations","tryThis":"Give a short list of what to look for (slang, tense shift, missing apostrophe). Have students underline one suspect word per sentence before rewriting."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Have students write one informal sentence about Odysseus and trade it with a partner to revise into formal language, naming the strategy used."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Students gather evidence from Chapter 22 and the Odyssey excerpt, then write a compare-and-contrast paragraph on what home means to each hero.","activities":[{"id":"lia-gather-evidence","title":"Part A: Cite Evidence from Two Homecomings","minutes":15,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.2","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 22","pages":"pp. 370-375"},{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Odyssey, Book 13 (excerpt)","pages":"Odysseus recognizes Ithaca"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 370-375 of Chapter 22. Annotate details about Percy's feelings about home, his mother's choices and the decision about where to spend the year. Then read the Odyssey excerpt and annotate Odysseus's joy, his kissing the ground and his prayer to the nymphs. Record your evidence in a two-column chart labeled Percy and Odysseus, with a bottom row labeled What home means."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What details in Chapter 22 show how Percy feels about home and what his mother has done for him?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy feels tied to his mom and wants to be near her, but camp is where he belongs too. His mom makes choices to keep him safe and give him a good life, and he has to decide where to spend the year."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What details show how Odysseus feels when he finally recognizes Ithaca?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"He is full of joy. He rejoices at being in his own land again, kisses the ground and prays to the nymphs. His actions show how much he has longed for his homeland."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is similar and what is different about how each hero returns home? What does that suggest about what home means to each?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Both heroes have been through dangerous journeys and both care deeply about home. For Odysseus, home is a place, his land, and he celebrates it with a ritual. For Percy, home is more about his mother and a choice between two places."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Before class, reread pp. 370-375 so you can confirm Percy's final decision about where to spend the year, and make sure students quote or paraphrase it accurately in their charts."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.9"],"stem":"Which detail from the Odyssey excerpt best shows Odysseus's joy at returning home?","choices":[{"text":"He kisses the soil and prays to the nymphs after he recognizes Ithaca.","correct":true,"rationale":"Kissing the ground and praying are actions that show his joy and gratitude at being home."},{"text":"He decides where to spend the year with his mother.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is Percy's decision in Chapter 22, not a detail from the Odyssey excerpt."},{"text":"He is afraid he has landed in a strange country.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is a believable mix-up because Odysseus does not recognize Ithaca at first, but the excerpt shows him rejoicing once he does."},{"text":"He feels unsure whether to stay or leave again.","correct":false,"rationale":"This describes Percy's choice in Chapter 22; Odysseus shows no doubt about being home."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in citing details from two texts and comparing them orally.","sayAsk":"Say: Point to the sentence, read it aloud, then say what it shows. Frames: In Chapter 22, Percy feels ___ because ___. In the Odyssey, Odysseus shows his joy when he ___. Both heroes ___, but Percy ___ while Odysseus ___. Add adverbials: Odysseus kisses the ground joyfully, in his homeland, after years away.","watchFor":"If students retell the plot without evidence, then ask: Which words in the text show that? If students mix up the two heroes, then have them label each detail P or O in the chart. Success: students cite at least one detail per hero and state one similarity or difference."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding details in the Odyssey excerpt","tryThis":"Read the excerpt aloud together, pausing after each action so students can underline joy, kissing the ground and prayer."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to infer why Odysseus prays to the nymphs and what that shows about his values, citing a detail."}]}]},{"id":"lia-draft-comparison","title":"Part B: Draft a Compare-and-Contrast Paragraph","minutes":15,"standards":["W.6.2","W.6.4","RL.6.9","L.6.1.e"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"I start with a topic sentence that names both heroes and the big idea: both return home, but home means something different to each. Then I give one detail from Chapter 22, one from the Odyssey, and use comparison transitions like *similarly*, *in contrast* and *whereas*. I use precise words, keep a formal style, and end with a sentence that explains what the comparison shows about their families and values. Last, I reread aloud and fix any slang or tense shifts."},{"type":"directions","text":"Use your chart to write a paragraph that answers: How is Percy's idea of coming home similar to and different from Odysseus's, and why? Include a topic sentence, at least one text detail for each hero, two comparison transitions, and a concluding sentence about family situations and values. Underline your transitions. Then reread aloud and revise one variation from standard English."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does home mean to Percy versus Odysseus, and how do their families explain the difference?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Home is a place to Odysseus, his homeland, which he has missed for years. Percy's home is tied to his mother and the choices she makes for him. They are different because Odysseus returns as a king to his land, and Percy is a kid deciding between his mom and camp."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Sample paragraph: Both Percy and Odysseus return home after dangerous journeys, but home means something different to each hero. In the Odyssey, Odysseus rejoices when he recognizes Ithaca, kisses the soil and prays to the nymphs, which shows that home is his homeland. In contrast, Percy's return in Chapter 22 centers on his mother's choices and his decision about where to spend the year, so home is tied to family and belonging. Similarly, both heroes value home deeply. However, Odysseus honors a place with ritual, whereas Percy weighs people he loves. These differences reflect their situations: a king long gone from his land and a boy deciding where he belongs."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Checklist: a topic sentence naming both heroes and the idea of home; one text detail for each hero; comparison transitions such as similarly, in contrast, whereas; precise language and a formal style; a concluding statement; no slang or tense shifts."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Circulate and conference with two or three students. Use the L.6.1.e check from the Literacy Lab: ask a student to read one sentence aloud and listen for slang or a tense shift."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in writing a comparison paragraph with transitions, formal language and adverbial detail.","sayAsk":"Say: First tell your partner your comparison in everyday words, then say it in formal school language. Frames: Both ___ and ___ return home, but ___. In the Odyssey, Odysseus ___ . In contrast, Percy ___ . Similarly, ___ . Adverbials: Percy decides carefully, in the final chapter, because he loves his mother.","watchFor":"If students list details about only one hero, then ask: What does the other text show? If students use only 'and' or 'but', then offer similarly, in contrast, whereas. If students copy sentences, then say: Close the book and tell the idea in your own words first. Success: students compare both heroes with at least one detail and one transition for each."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: starting the paragraph","tryThis":"Offer this starter: Both Percy and Odysseus return home, but ___ means something different to each. Have students draft one sentence at a time and rehearse it aloud first."},{"type":"situation-placeholder-removed","tryThis":"unused"},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Challenge students to add a sentence explaining how the heroes' family situations shape their values, and to replace a basic word like shows with a more precise one such as reveals or illustrates."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on how comparing two texts and using formal language strengthens their writing.","activities":[{"id":"lookback-turn-and-talk","title":"Why Compare Two Homecomings?","minutes":5,"standards":["W.6.4","L.6.1.e"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Share one sentence from your paragraph with a partner. Tell what you revised to make it more formal and conventional."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does comparing Percy's story with Odysseus's help you understand the idea of home?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Seeing both heroes shows that home can mean a place or people. Odysseus's joy is about his land, but Percy's is about his mom, so the two stories show different values."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In your Performance Task you will compare two stories the same way: use evidence from each, connect them with clear transitions and write in a formal style."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Prepare for the Academic Discussion in Lesson 35.","activities":[{"id":"homework-prepare","title":"Prepare for the Discussion","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Review your annotations from The Lightning Thief and the myths you read in Investigations 1 and 2. Star two places where a story's ideas about heroes or home connect. Then watch the clips from the movie version of The Lightning Thief that your teacher chooses, and jot down one way the movie differs from the novel."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students cite details from Chapter 22 of The Lightning Thief (pp. 370-375) and the Odyssey Book 13 excerpt to compare how Percy and Odysseus return home and what home means to each, then write a compare-and-contrast paragraph. A Literacy Lab on recognizing variations from standard English and revising to conventional, formal language supports the writing.","keyActivities":["Launch Turn and Talk: What Does Home Mean?","Language Study: recognizing variations from standard English (L.6.1.e)","Part A: annotating and charting evidence from Chapter 22 and the Odyssey excerpt","Part B: Quick Write of a compare-and-contrast paragraph with transitions and formal style","Look Back Turn and Talk on revising for formal language"],"vocabularyTaught":["variation","conventional","contrast","depict","rejoice","nymph"],"standardsCovered":["W.6.2","W.6.4","RL.6.1","RL.6.2","RL.6.9","L.6.1","L.6.1.e"]}}
